title: Emergence of Subdominant Quadrupolar Order in the 5$d^2$ Multipolar Mott Insulator Ba$_2$CaOsO$_6$
authors: Ilija K. Nikolov, Giuseppe Allodi, Ginevra Corsale, Anshu Kataria, Cierra Foster, Patrick Woodward, Samuele Sanna, Vesna F. Mitrović
abstract: Relativistic $5d$ Mott insulators host a rich variety of exotic hidden multipolar order, whose microscopic nature remains heavily debated. A broken local point-symmetry (BLPS) phase followed by antiferromagnetism was previously observed in the doped compound Ba$_2$Na$_{0.1}$Ca$_{0.9}$OsO$_6$, where mixed Os valence places the system toward the $5d^2$ end of the $5d^1$-$5d^2$ regime. In contrast, pristine $5d^2$ Ba$_2$CaOsO$_6$ has shown a single octupolar transition with average cubic symmetry, raising the question of whether BLPS arises from chemical disorder in the doped systems. Here, we discover the BLPS phase in pristine Ba$_2$CaOsO$_6$ emerging at $T^* \approx 50$ K, precisely coincident with the octupolar transition. Beyond standard ${}^{43}$Ca nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectral analysis, our spin-echo nutation measurements detect a finite electric field gradient, demonstrating spontaneous symmetry breaking despite the cubic average structure. While our NMR data support the previously identified octupolar order, the BLPS phase reveals a subdominant quadrupolar contribution, establishing that the hidden order in Ba$_2$CaOsO$_6$ is intrinsically multicomponent. Such mixed multipolar states lie beyond conventional theoretical descriptions of the $5d^2$ ground state. Our results establish local symmetry breaking as an intrinsic property of the clean $5d^2$ limit and provide a new constraint on microscopic theories of strongly spin-orbit-coupled Mott insulators.
summary: This experimental work investigates the exotic hidden order in the $5d^2$ Mott insulator $	ext{Ba}_2	ext{CaOsO}_6$ using advanced NMR techniques. The researchers found that the material undergoes a transition at $T^* \approx 50$ K, which breaks local symmetry. Crucially, they established that the hidden order is not purely octupolar, but rather a mixed state containing a subdominant quadrupolar component.
main_problem: The paper investigates the nature of exotic hidden multipolar order in the $5d^2$ Mott insulator $	ext{Ba}_2	ext{CaOsO}_6$, specifically determining if the order is intrinsically multicomponent.
main_result: The authors discovered that the hidden order in pristine $	ext{Ba}_2	ext{CaOsO}_6$ is intrinsically multicomponent, consisting of a dominant octupolar order coexisting with a subdominant quadrupolar contribution.
method: The study employed advanced local probes, primarily ${}^{43}	ext{Ca}$ Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) measurements, alongside bulk magnetic characterization.
model_or_system: The physical system is the double-perovskite Mott insulator $	ext{Ba}_2	ext{CaOsO}_6$, which is characterized as a $5d^2$ system exhibiting strong spin-orbit coupling.
key_observables: NMR line broadening (indicating finite Electric Field Gradient, EFG), spectral asymmetry/skewness, and anomalies in magnetic susceptibility ($\chi$) at $T^* \approx 50$ K.
important_parameters: The transition temperature $T^* \approx 50$ K, and the energy scale associated with the electronic structure ($\Delta_c \approx 22 	ext{ meV}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the NMR measurements provide a unique, non-perturbative local probe sensitive to spontaneous symmetry breaking, even when the average structure remains cubic.
figures_summary: Figures show NMR spectra broadening below $T^*$, magnetic susceptibility anomalies, and evidence of spectral bifurcation between the NMR mode and the first moment, all occurring at $T^*$.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the context of multipolar order in $5d$ Mott insulators, presents evidence from NMR and magnetometry showing a transition at $T^*$, and concludes that the local symmetry breaking implies a mixed, multicomponent multipolar ground state.
why_interesting: The detection of a subdominant quadrupolar component alongside octupolar order in a clean Mott insulator provides crucial, detailed constraints for theoretical models attempting to describe complex, high-order multipolar interactions in strongly correlated systems.
